verdict.summary:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — OXYGEN-DEFICIENT AND OXYGEN-ENRICHED ATMOSPHERES UNDER 29 CFR 1910.146(b), JULY 1, 2014 EDITION

1. ANSWERS

| Ask | Term defined in 1910.146(b) | Threshold | Comparison operator | Concentration basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Oxygen deficient atmosphere | 19.5 | strictly less than (<) | percent oxygen by volume (v/v) |
| 2 | Oxygen enriched atmosphere | 23.5 | strictly greater than (>) | percent oxygen by volume (v/v) |
| 3 (constraint) | Operators and basis | — | '<' for deficient, '>' for enriched; neither is inclusive | percent by volume of oxygen in the atmosphere sampled |

2. VERBATIM REGULATORY TEXT (29 CFR 1910.146(b), as revised as of July 1, 2014; Title 29 CFR Volume 5)

"Oxygen deficient atmosphere means an atmosphere containing less than 19.5 percent oxygen by volume."

"Oxygen enriched atmosphere means an atmosphere containing more than 23.5 percent oxygen by volume."

These are the two definitional sentences in 1910.146(b); the section's definitional paragraph is alphabetical, and both entries appear as quoted. The text was verified against the archived annual edition PDF for July 1, 2014 (CFR-2014-title29-vol5-sec1910-146.pdf, fetched 2026-11-15T04:13:06Z, sha256 a53232848d11), and is identical to the current eCFR and OSHA-published text of 1910.146(b). No amendment in the window changed these figures.

3. COMPARISON OPERATORS — COMPLIANCE BOUNDARY

- Deficient uses "less than": O2 < 19.5 percent by volume. A reading of exactly 19.5 percent is NOT oxygen-deficient under this definition.
- Enriched uses "more than": O2 > 23.5 percent by volume. A reading of exactly 23.5 percent is NOT oxygen-enriched under this definition.
- Do not restate either as '<=' or '>='. Writing '19.5 percent or less' or '23.5 percent or more' shifts the compliance boundary by one endpoint and is a citation error; enforcement and instrument tolerance discussions turn on exactly these endpoints.
- Combined effect: the standard treats 19.5 percent <= O2 <= 23.5 percent by volume as the non-deficient, non-enriched band. This is consistent with 1910.146(b)'s definition of "hazardous atmosphere," which includes an atmosphere with an oxygen concentration below 19.5 percent or above 23.5 percent, and with the oxygen-testing range used in the standard's entry procedures (Appendix B to 1910.146, which directs testing for oxygen in the 19.5 to 23.5 percent range).
- There is no gap and no overlap between the two definitions: 19.5 < 23.5, and the interval between them is assigned to neither term.

4. CONCENTRATION BASIS

The basis stated in both definitions is percent oxygen by volume — a volume/volume concentration of oxygen in the atmosphere being evaluated. Consequences to preserve when applying or restating the rule:
- It is not percent by weight/mass, not mole percent expressed on a dry basis with a correction the rule does not state, and not partial pressure.
- The basis is the atmosphere actually sampled at the point of measurement (the confined space's internal atmosphere), not ambient outdoor air or a supplied-air stream.
- The figures are percentage-of-atmosphere values, so they remain the applicable thresholds regardless of the instrument used, provided the instrument reports oxygen in percent by volume (direct-reading oxygen meters do).
- 1910.146(b) does not separately define "oxygen" or prescribe a measurement method; instrument selection, calibration, and sampling protocol come from the employer's confined-space program and 1910.146(d) / Appendix B, not from the (b) definitions.

5. SCOPE AND NON-CONFLATION NOTES

- This determination is specific to 29 CFR 1910.146(b), OSHA's permit-required confined spaces standard in general industry. It is not a statement of oxygen-deficiency thresholds used in other OSHA standards (for example respiratory-protection or construction standards) or in industrial-hygiene practice generally; those should be cited from their own text rather than from 1910.146.
- 1910.146(b) supplies the definitions; the enforceable obligation to test and to keep the atmosphere within the band arises elsewhere in the section (the employer's written program, pre-entry and periodic testing, and acceptable entry conditions).

6. SUGGESTED CITATION FORM

29 CFR 1910.146(b) (2014) (Oxygen deficient atmosphere; Oxygen enriched atmosphere), as published in 29 C.F.R. pt. 1910 (rev. July 1, 2014). If a current citation is preferred, the same text appears in the current eCFR at 29 CFR 1910.146(b); no edition conflict needs to be disclosed because the two texts are identical for these two definitions.

7. QUALIFICATIONS

No assumption beyond the verified text is needed to state the two values, the operators, or the basis. Nothing in this answer depends on a figure not quoted above.

DOCUMENTATION RECORD — MCLs under 40 CFR § 141.62 for a community water system (July 1, 2014 edition of the CFR)

1. ANSWER
   • Arsenic — 0.010 mg/L
   • Fluoride — 4.0 mg/L
   • Nitrate — 10 mg/L, reported AS NITROGEN (the table entry reads "Nitrate | 10 (as Nitrogen)")
   All three are maximum contaminant levels (MCLs), National Primary Drinking Water Regulations, 40 CFR Part 141, and are expressed in milligrams per liter (mg/L) exactly as the regulation expresses them. No unit conversion is performed in the answer itself.

2. DATA RECORD (for the documentation file)
   Field | Value
   Regulation | 40 CFR Part 141, National Primary Drinking Water Regulations
   Section | § 141.62, Maximum contaminant levels for inorganic contaminants
   Edition | Code of Federal Regulations, Title 40, revised as of July 1, 2014 (annual edition)
   System type | Community water system (same table also governs non-transient non-community systems)
   
   Contaminant | MCL | Unit | Reporting basis | Row in § 141.62 table | Verification
   Arsenic | 0.010 | mg/L | as total arsenic (elemental basis; no speciation) | row (16) | value stable since 23 Jan 2006; present in the 2014 edition
   Fluoride | 4.0 | mg/L | as fluoride ion (F-) | row (1) | value unchanged since the 1985/86 fluoride regulation
   Nitrate | 10 | mg/L | AS NITROGEN (N) — stated in the table itself | row (7) | value and basis unchanged since the 1975 interim regulations

3. TABLE TRANSCRIPTION (relevant rows, with the neighbouring nitrogen rows retained because they are routinely confused with the nitrate MCL)
   | Contaminant | MCL (mg/L) |
   | (1) Fluoride | 4.0 |
   | (7) Nitrate | 10 (as Nitrogen) |
   | (8) Nitrite | 1 (as Nitrogen) |
   | (9) Total Nitrate and Nitrite | 10 (as Nitrogen) |
   | (14) [Reserved] | — |
   | (16) Arsenic | 0.010 |
   The table runs (1) through (16); row (14) is reserved and carries no MCL (it is the slot vacated when lead regulation moved to the lead and copper treatment-technique rule). Nitrate (row 7), nitrite (row 8) and total nitrate plus nitrite (row 9) are three separate entries with three separate MCLs; the requested entry is row (7) only.

4. CHEMICAL REPORTING BASIS FOR NITRATE (ask 3)
   The regulation states the basis on the face of the MCL table: nitrate is limited at "10 (as Nitrogen)". The regulatory concentration is therefore 10 mg/L expressed as elemental nitrogen, not as nitrate ion (NO3-).
   Derived conversion, for annotation only and NOT a regulatory value: 10 mg/L as N x (62.005 g/mol NO3 / 14.007 g/mol N) = 44.3 mg/L as NO3. Do not report "10 mg/L as NO3" — that would understate the regulated concentration by a factor of about 4.43. Conversely, a laboratory result reported as 44.3 mg/L NO3 is at the MCL, not 4.43 times above it.

5. EDITION CONTROL — WHY THE JULY 1, 2014 TEXT CARRIES THESE VALUES
   Arsenic: the MCL was 0.05 mg/L under the 1975 interim regulations and was lowered to 0.010 mg/L by the arsenic rule published at 66 FR 6976 (Jan. 22, 2001), with compliance required from 23 Jan. 2006. The July 1, 2014 edition therefore reads 0.010, and no arsenic MCL amendment occurred between 2006 and 2014.
   Fluoride: MCL 4.0 mg/L has been in place since the mid-1980s fluoride regulation and was not amended between then and 2014.
   Nitrate: MCL 10 mg/L as N dates from the 1975 interim regulations; the nitrite (1, as N) and total nitrate/nitrite (10, as N) rows were added by the Phase II rule (56 FR 3526, Jan. 30, 1991). Neither the nitrate value nor its "as Nitrogen" basis changed between 1991 and 2014.
   Conclusion: no amendment in the 2006-2014 window could have altered the three requested values, so the July 1, 2014 edition necessarily reads 0.010 / 4.0 / 10 (as N).

6. VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (to close the citation before publication)
   Step 1. Retrieve the annual edition, not e-CFR: e-CFR point-in-time browsing does not reach 2014. Use GovInfo > Code of Federal Regulations > 2014 edition > Title 40 > the volume containing Part 141 (Part 141 has sat in volume 25 in recent years; confirm the volume's part range on its title page before citing). Package naming follows the pattern CFR-2014-title40-volNN; the XML/PDF section file for § 141.62 is the primary artifact.
   Step 2. Read § 141.62 and confirm which paragraph holds the 16-row MCL table. The retrieved rendering places it in paragraph (b), and EPA's published NPDWR contaminant table cites § 141.62(b) for these inorganics. If the page image instead shows the table under paragraph (a), the three values are unchanged — only the letter in the citation string changes. Flag this letter in the file as the one item confirmed from a rendering rather than a page image.
   Step 3. Confirm no intervening amendment with the List of CFR Sections Affiliated (LSA) cumulative issue for 2014, checking the entry for 40 CFR 141.62.
   Step 4. Record in the file: edition date, section, paragraph, row numbers, retrieval date, and the source artifact identifier.

7. SCOPE / APPLICABILITY NOTE
   § 141.62 is the inorganic MCL table. It is the table that applies to community water systems (and to non-transient non-community systems); transient non-community systems are governed by the narrower set of entries in § 141.62(b) — fluoride, nitrate, nitrite and total nitrate/nitrite — and are not subject to the arsenic MCL. If the answer is being reused for a transient non-community system, drop arsenic and keep 4.0 / 10 (as N).

8. CITATION STRINGS READY FOR USE
   Short: 40 CFR § 141.62(b) (2014).
   Full: 40 C.F.R. § 141.62(b) (2014) (maximum contaminant levels for inorganic contaminants), as revised July 1, 2014.
   With values: 40 C.F.R. § 141.62(b) (2014) (arsenic 0.010 mg/L; fluoride 4.0 mg/L; nitrate 10 mg/L as N).

9. DO-NOT-CONFUSE LIST (kept with the record so downstream users do not misread the numbers)
   • Fluoride 4.0 mg/L is the MCL; 2.0 mg/L is the SECONDARY maximum contaminant level (40 CFR § 143.3), a different, non-enforceable aesthetics standard. Do not substitute 2.0.
   • Arsenic 0.010 mg/L = 10 µg/L. Same value, different scale; do not write "10 mg/L".
   • Nitrate 10 (as N) is not nitrite 1 (as N) and is not the combined total nitrate/nitrite entry, which is also 10 (as N) but is a distinct row.
   • "As N" applies to nitrate, nitrite and total nitrate/nitrite only. Arsenic and fluoride carry no nitrogen basis.

10. STATUS
   Asks 1-3 answered. Value confidence high (stable, uncontested across editions). Residual item: page-image confirmation of the paragraph letter (a) vs (b) for the citation string only; it does not affect any numeric value or the reporting basis.

verdict.summary:
SAFETY ENGINEER — REGULATORY DETERMINATION
Authority: 29 CFR § 1910.95(g), Occupational Noise Exposure — Audiometric Testing Program, as codified in the July 1, 2014 edition of the CFR. The figures below are taken verbatim from that text; where a printing differs only in paragraph designations or formatting, the quoted language controls and the figures are unchanged.

1. ANSWER TABLE

| # | Question | Answer | Unit | Nature of the limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Deadline to establish a baseline audiogram after first exposure at or above the action level, mobile-test-van exception NOT used | 6 | months | Maximum (latest permissible date); earlier is compliant and preferred |
| 2 | Minimum workplace-noise-free period preceding a baseline audiogram when hearing protectors are NOT used as a substitute | 14 | hours | Minimum (floor); 'at least 14 hours' |
| 3 | Allowed retest window after an annual audiogram shows a standard threshold shift | 30 | days | Maximum window; retest is permissive, not required |

2. CONTROLLING TEXT AND CITATION MAP

Ask 1 — Baseline audiogram deadline (general rule):
"Within 6 months of an employee's first exposure at or above the action level, the employer shall establish a valid baseline audiogram against which subsequent audiograms can be compared."
Cited as § 1910.95(g)(5).

Ask 1 — The excluded exception (stated only to show it does not apply here):
"Mobile test van exception. Where mobile test vans are used to meet the audiometric testing obligation, the employer shall obtain a valid baseline audiogram within 1 year of an employee's first exposure at or above the action level."
Cited as § 1910.95(g)(5)(i). Because the request specifies the exception is not used, the 1-year figure is not the answer and must not be applied. It is mutually exclusive with the 6-month rule, not cumulative.

Ask 2 — Noise-free interval:
"Testing to establish a baseline audiogram shall be preceded by at least 14 hours without exposure to workplace noise. Hearing protectors may be used as a substitute for the requirement that baseline audiograms be preceded by 14 hours without exposure to workplace noise."
Cited as § 1910.95(g)(6).

Ask 3 — Retest after a standard threshold shift:
"If the annual audiogram shows that an employee has suffered a standard threshold shift, the employer may obtain a retest within 30 days and consider the results of the retest as the annual audiogram."
Cited as § 1910.95(g)(10)(i).

Context anchors (not answers, listed so the triggers are unambiguous): action level = 8-hour time-weighted average of 85 dBA; permissible exposure limit = 90 dBA 8-hour TWA; standard threshold shift = change relative to the baseline of an average of 10 dB or more at 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz in either ear.

3. APPLICATION RULES — HOW EACH FIGURE IS APPLIED

Rule 1 (6 months). The clock starts on the date of first exposure at or above the action level, not the hire date, not the date the exposure assessment was completed, and not the date the audiogram is scheduled. 'Within 6 months' means calendar months from that date. The baseline must be a valid audiogram (tested per the instrument and technician requirements of the standard, and preceded by the quiet period in Rule 2). If the baseline is established late, the audiogram is still required and still becomes the comparison audiogram, but the interval of unmonitored exposure is a documented compliance gap. Do not treat the 6-month figure as a target to be filled; schedule as early as practicable after the exposure determination.

Rule 2 (14 hours). When hearing protectors are not used as the substitute, the employee must have at least 14 consecutive hours with no exposure to workplace noise immediately before the baseline test. This is a minimum: 14 hours exactly is compliant, 12 hours is not, and 16 hours is better. 'No exposure to workplace noise' means no on-site noise exposure during the interval — the interval is a workplace-noise-free period, so the practical control is to schedule the test at the start of a shift following a full off-duty period and to confirm the employee performed no noisy work in the preceding 14 hours (overtime, call-in, on-call maintenance, or a second job at a noisy site all break the interval). Hearing-protector substitution is the only relaxation the standard provides; the request excludes it, so the full 14 hours is mandatory and the audiogram should be rescheduled rather than run short. Document the quiet-period verification on the testing record (employee attestation plus scheduling evidence).

Rule 3 (30 days). The 30-day window opens on the date of the annual audiogram that shows the standard threshold shift and closes 30 calendar days later. Within that window the employer may retest and, if it does, may treat the retest result as the annual audiogram. Two limits must be stated plainly: (a) the retest is permissive — the employer is not obligated to retest, and choosing not to retest does not excuse the follow-up obligations that attach to a confirmed shift; (b) a retest obtained after the 30-day window cannot be substituted for the annual audiogram under this provision. The retest is a substitution mechanism for the annual audiogram result, not a mechanism for erasing the shift.

4. IMPLEMENTATION PROCEDURE (site level)

Step 1 — Fix the trigger date. From the exposure assessment, record the first date any employee is exposed at or above the 85 dBA 8-hour TWA action level. Store it as the baseline-clock start date in the hearing conservation record.
Step 2 — Compute the baseline deadline. Deadline = trigger date + 6 calendar months. Enter it as a hard date, not a relative one.
Step 3 — Schedule with quiet-period margin. Book the audiogram on or before the deadline, at the start of a shift, with a verified 14-hour workplace-noise-free interval. If the earliest available slot cannot satisfy both the deadline and the 14-hour interval, move the test earlier, not later; a test that violates the quiet period is not a valid baseline and does not satisfy the deadline.
Step 4 — Mobile test van check. Only if the testing is actually delivered by a mobile test van may the 1-year deadline be used instead of 6 months. Record the basis. Absent that, the 6-month deadline governs.
Step 5 — Annual audiogram review. On each annual audiogram, evaluate against the baseline for a standard threshold shift. If a shift is recorded, open a 30-day retest clock on the audiogram date.
Step 6 — Retest decision. Within the 30 days, either obtain the retest and record it as the annual audiogram, or record the decision not to retest and proceed with the follow-up obligations. A retest obtained after day 30 is recorded as a separate test, not as the annual audiogram.
Step 7 — Record retention and audit. Retain the trigger date, the deadline computation, the quiet-period verification, and the retest date/decision so each of the three clocks can be reconstructed on inspection.

5. COMMON ERRORS THIS DETERMINATION GUARDS AGAINST
- Applying the 1-year mobile-van figure when no mobile test van was used (the single most common misreading of (g)(5)).
- Converting 6 months into a day count and then treating the converted figure as the requirement; the standard states months.
- Running a baseline after only an overnight gap that is shorter than 14 hours, or counting non-workplace quiet as a substitute when protectors are not used — neither satisfies (g)(6).
- Treating the 30-day retest as mandatory, or treating a late retest as the annual audiogram.
- Restarting the 6-month clock at the date of the exposure assessment or the date of hire rather than the date of first exposure at or above the action level.

6. BOUNDARIES OF THIS ANSWER
This determination covers the three figures requested under the federal standard as of the July 1, 2014 edition. It does not address state-plan variants, other regulatory regimes (e.g., MSHA or FRA noise rules), OSHA letters of interpretation, or amendments after that edition; those would need separate confirmation and could alter application, though not the three figures as quoted. Paragraph designations are given for navigation; if a particular printing numbers them differently, the verbatim language quoted in Section 2 is the controlling text.

  95 dBA  ->  4 hours per day
 100 dBA  ->  2 hours per day

BASIS
1. Direct table lookup. Table G-16 is a two-column table: duration per day (hours) and sound level (dBA, slow response). The rows covering the requested levels are: 8 h / 90 dBA; 6 h / 92 dBA; 4 h / 95 dBA; 3 h / 97 dBA; 2 h / 100 dBA; 1.5 h / 102 dBA; 1 h / 105 dBA; 0.5 h / 110 dBA; 0.25 h or less / 115 dBA. 2. Arithmetic cross-check against the 5-dB exchange rate the table embodies. Table G-16 follows T = 8 / 2^((L - 90)/5), where T is the permissible duration in hours and L is the slow-response A-weighted level in dBA:
   L = 90 : T = 8 / 2^0 = 8 h
   L = 95 : T = 8 / 2^1 = 4 h
   L = 100: T = 8 / 2^2 = 2 h
Both routes give the same three numbers, so the reported values agree with the table's own governing relation and with each other.

# Oxygen deficiency and oxygen enrichment thresholds — 29 CFR § 1910.146(b), July 1, 2014 edition

## 1. Answer — verbatim regulatory definitions

Governing text: 29 CFR Part 1910, § 1910.146 "Permit-required confined spaces," paragraph (b) "Definitions," as published in the Code of Federal Regulations, Title 29, Volume 5, revised as of July 1, 2014 (GovInfo file CFR-2014-title29-vol5, section 1910.146).

> "Oxygen deficient atmosphere means an atmosphere containing **less than 19.5 percent oxygen by volume**."
>
> "Oxygen enriched atmosphere means an atmosphere containing **more than 23.5 percent oxygen by volume**."

(Reproduced as printed. Note that the regulatory text spells the defined terms without hyphens — "oxygen deficient" and "oxygen enriched" — although practitioners commonly write "oxygen-deficient" and "oxygen-enriched.")

## 2. Threshold table — operators and concentration basis

| Defined term | Comparison operator | Threshold | Concentration basis | At exactly the threshold |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Oxygen deficient atmosphere | **less than** (`<`) — strict | **19.5** | percent oxygen **by volume** | 19.5% is **not** oxygen deficient |
| Oxygen enriched atmosphere | **more than** (`>`) — strict | **23.5** | percent oxygen **by volume** | 23.5% is **not** oxygen enriched |

Concentration band to which neither defined term applies: **19.5% ≤ O2 ≤ 23.5%** (percent oxygen by volume).

## 3. Operator analysis and boundary cases

Both operators are strict. The definitions do not say "less than or equal to," "at or below," "not more than," or "at or above." Consequently the boundaries themselves are excluded from both defined terms.

| Reading (% O2 by volume) | Oxygen deficient? | Oxygen enriched? |
|---|---|---|
| 19.4 | Yes (19.4 < 19.5) | No |
| 19.5 | No (boundary) | No |
| 20.9 (normal air) | No | No |
| 23.5 | No | No (boundary) |
| 23.6 | No | Yes (23.6 > 23.5) |

Practical consequence for a safety program: a space reading exactly 19.5% or exactly 23.5% is outside both legal definitions, but is at the edge of them. Direct-reading electrochemical oxygen instruments have finite accuracy, so a reading sitting on a boundary should be treated conservatively (as deficient, or as enriched) until confirmed by a calibrated instrument and repeat measurement. That is a conservative operating practice layered on top of the definition — it does not change the definition, which remains strictly `< 19.5` and `> 23.5`. Similarly, an instrument whose alarm logic trips at "19.5% or below" or "23.5% or above" is slightly more conservative than the regulatory text; that divergence is acceptable and should be documented rather than "corrected" to match the boundary exactly.

## 4. Concentration basis

- The basis is **percent oxygen by volume** — the volumetric fraction of oxygen in the atmosphere multiplied by 100. It is not percent by mass, and it is not oxygen partial pressure.
- The definitions do not specify a dry-gas or humid-gas basis, and they do not specify a temperature or pressure correction; they are applied to the atmosphere as measured by a calibrated direct-reading instrument.
- Because the basis is volumetric, the definitions do not by themselves address the case of a space at altitude (or with reduced barometric pressure) that reads an acceptable volumetric percentage while the oxygen partial pressure is low. § 1910.146(b) does not resolve that case; do not use these two definitions as the sole acceptance criterion where partial pressure is the controlling hazard.

## 5. Related provisions in the same section and edition (context only — not the (b) definitions)

- **§ 1910.146(b), "Hazardous atmosphere," item (3)** lists as one cause of a hazardous atmosphere an "atmospheric oxygen concentration below 19.5 percent or above 23.5 percent." The numbers are identical to the two definitions; only the phrasing differs ("below/above" rather than "less than/more than"). This is a separate defined term used to trigger permit-space controls, not a third threshold.
- **§ 1910.146(c)(5)(ii)(C)** requires pre-entry testing with a calibrated direct-reading instrument for oxygen content first, then flammable gases and vapors, then potential toxic air contaminants — the operational reason the oxygen definitions sit first in the testing sequence.
- **Appendix B to § 1910.146, "Procedures for Atmospheric Testing,"** elaborates on testing order, instrument calibration, and evaluation of results. It supplies procedure, not different numeric limits.
- Cross-references above are provided as operational context. For enforcement or citation purposes, verify paragraph-level cross-references against the same July 1, 2014 edition; the two (b) definitions quoted in section 1 are the answer to this request.

## 6. Provenance and verification

- Text quoted from the GovInfo PDF of 29 CFR Ch. XVII, part 1910, § 1910.146, revised as of July 1, 2014 (retrieved in the research pass; file hash recorded as sha256 `a53232848d11`).
- Internal consistency check: the (b) deficiency/enrichment definitions (19.5 / 23.5) agree numerically with the (b) "hazardous atmosphere" criterion (below 19.5 / above 23.5). No conflicting figure appears in the deliverable.
- No intervening amendment to these two definitions was identified between the July 1, 2014 edition and the current eCFR text retrieved in the same research pass. This is a consistency observation, not a legal opinion on later editions.
- Cross-check only (verify independently if relied on): the same 19.5% / 23.5% pair appears in 29 CFR § 1910.134(b) (respiratory protection) and in 29 CFR § 1926.1202 (construction confined spaces). Those are different standards; they do not modify § 1910.146(b).

## 7. Scope, assumptions, and limits

- Answers are the definitions as written in the July 1, 2014 edition, quoted verbatim; no paraphrase is substituted for the operative language.
- The request's ask 3 (comparison operators and concentration basis) is a constraint on the answer, not a separate numeric value; it is discharged by the verbatim operators ("less than," "more than") in section 1 and by "percent oxygen by volume" in sections 1, 2, and 4.
- Out of scope and not answered here: employer-specific entry limits tighter than the regulatory floor, instrument selection/calibration specifications, ventilation design, and rescue provisions. These belong to § 1910.146(c)–(k), Appendix B, and § 1910.134, and should be developed separately against the same edition.
- Bottom line for the record: oxygen deficient = **less than 19.5 percent oxygen by volume**; oxygen enriched = **more than 23.5 percent oxygen by volume**; both operators strict; basis is volumetric percent oxygen.

COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — 40 CFR § 141.62(b), July 1, 2014 edition

1. ANSWER (MCLs, § 141.62(b), community water systems, mg/L)

  Contaminant | MCL as printed in § 141.62(b) | Reported in mg/L
  Arsenic     | 0.010                      | 0.010 mg/L
  Fluoride    | 4.0                        | 4.0 mg/L
  Nitrate     | 10 (as Nitrogen)           | 10 mg/L as N

  Table position of each entry in the § 141.62(b) inorganic-contaminant table, as numbered: (1) Fluoride, (7) Nitrate, (16) Arsenic. Values are quoted at the precision printed in the regulation: fluoride to one decimal (4.0), nitrate to whole numbers (10), arsenic to three decimals (0.010). Do not re-round: arsenic is 0.010, not 0.01, in the printed table, and compliance is determined at 0.010 mg/L.

2. REPORTING BASIS FOR NITRATE (the third ask)

  The regulation specifies the basis inline in the table cell itself: "Nitrate | 10 (as Nitrogen)". The MCL is therefore 10 mg/L expressed as nitrogen (as N) — a nitrogen-mass basis, NOT a nitrate-ion (NO3) basis. This is not a footnote and not an inference; the parenthetical is part of the MCL entry. The adjacent inorganic-nitrogen entries use the same basis — (8) Nitrite 1 (as Nitrogen) and (9) Total Nitrate and Nitrite 10 (as Nitrogen) — so the whole inorganic-nitrogen group in this table is on an as-N basis.

  Practical consequence for a CWS (this is the step practitioners most often get wrong): a laboratory result reported as nitrate ion must be converted before comparison with the 10 mg/L MCL.
    Conversion factor: M(NO3)/M(N) = 62.005/14.007 = 4.427
    NO3 (mg/L) = N (mg/L) × 4.427
    10 mg/L as N  =  44.27 mg/L as NO3
  So the MCL is 10 mg/L as N, which is numerically identical to 44.27 mg/L as NO3. A result of, e.g., 40 mg/L as NO3 is 40/4.427 = 9.04 mg/L as N — below the MCL — whereas 40 mg/L as N would be 177 mg/L as NO3 and far above it. Always record which basis the lab used; the regulation's basis is as N.

3. SCOPE AND QUALIFICATIONS

  - These are federal primary (enforceable) NPDWR MCLs under 40 CFR Part 141, Subpart G, applicable to community water systems. State-level primary standards may be equal to or stricter than these; this answer states the federal figures only.
  - Fluoride: 4.0 mg/L is the § 141.62(b) MCL. The 2.0 mg/L fluoride figure that circulates in practice is the non-enforceable secondary standard (40 CFR 143.3), a different part of the CFR; it must not be substituted for, or reported as, the MCL.
  - Nitrate: the 10 mg/L figure must never be reported without its basis. Reporting "10 mg/L nitrate" unqualified is ambiguous by a factor of 4.427.
  - No footnote in the table modifies these three values; the nitrogen basis appears inline in the nitrate cell.

4. EDITION-DATING CHECK (why the 2014 edition is safe to cite as above)

  The three values are stable across the window that brackets the July 1, 2014 edition:
  - Arsenic 0.010 mg/L took effect 23 January 2006 (Arsenic Rule, 66 FR 6976, published 22 January 2001; compliance date 2006). Any edition from 2006 onward — including July 1, 2014 — carries 0.010. Pre-2002 editions carry 0.05 mg/L; if a source shows 0.05 for arsenic, it is an older edition and is not the cited text.
  - Fluoride 4.0 mg/L and nitrate 10 mg/L as N have been unchanged since the 1986 amendments and the 1975 Interim Primary Drinking Water Regulations respectively, so both are unchanged in 2014.
  Therefore no amendment effective on or near July 1, 2014 alters any of the three figures or the nitrate basis.

  Traceability procedure for a reviewer who wants the verbatim 2014 text (recommended before filing): retrieve the annual edition volume CFR-2014-title40-vol25, section 141.62, from GovInfo (XML, PDF, or the bound-volume HTML) — not the current eCFR page — and confirm the table rows (1) Fluoride 4.0, (7) Nitrate 10 (as Nitrogen), (16) Arsenic 0.010. Note: the values above are corroborated by the section text available in the sources consulted, but the verbatim July 1, 2014 annual-volume page was not itself among the quoted passages; the edition-dating check in this section is what establishes that the corroborated values are the 2014 values, and the GovInfo 2014 volume is the document that closes that last gap.

5. HOW TO CITE

  40 CFR § 141.62(b) (2014) — Maximum contaminant levels for inorganic contaminants, table entries (1), (7), (16). Cite the edition: "40 CFR § 141.62(b) (July 1, 2014 ed.)".

6. STATEMENT OF LIMITS

  This is a regulatory-content determination for a community water system against the federal NPDWRs. It is not a compliance determination for any specific system: whether a given system exceeds these MCLs depends on its monitoring results, the analytical basis those results are reported on (see § 2), and any state primary standard that is stricter than the federal figure.

verdict.summary:
# Compliance determination — 29 CFR §1910.95(g) audiometric testing timeframes (July 1, 2014 edition)

**Scope and basis.** Federal OSHA occupational noise exposure standard, 29 CFR §1910.95(g), as published in the July 1, 2014 edition of 29 CFR Part 1910. The three requested timeframes are taken from the operative regulatory text quoted verbatim in Section 2. Those three provisions read the same in the current eCFR rendering of §1910.95 retrieved for this analysis, so no edition drift affects the answers; if your program is pinned to a different edition, re-verify Section 2 against that text before relying on Section 1.

## 1. Answers

| # | Question | Answer | Unit | Controlling provision |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Baseline audiogram deadline after first exposure at or above the action level; mobile-test-van exception not used | **6** | months, measured from the date of first exposure at or above the action level | §1910.95(g)(5)(i) |
| 2 | Minimum workplace-noise-free period before a baseline audiogram; hearing protectors not used as a substitute | **14** | hours without exposure to workplace noise, immediately preceding the test | §1910.95(g)(5)(iii) |
| 3 | Retest window after an annual audiogram shows a standard threshold shift (STS) | **30** | days, measured from the date of the annual audiogram | §1910.95(g)(7)(ii) |

How to read the three values: 6 months is a latest-permissible date (testing earlier is compliant, later is not); 14 hours is a minimum (longer is compliant and preferred); 30 days is an outer limit (an earlier retest is compliant).

## 2. Governing text

Verbatim, from 29 CFR §1910.95 (eCFR, https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-1910.95, retrieved 2026-11-15):

> §1910.95(g)(5)(i): “Within 6 months of an employee’s first exposure at or above the action level, the employer shall establish a valid baseline audiogram against which subsequent audiograms can be compared.”

> §1910.95(g)(5)(iii): “Testing to establish a baseline audiogram shall be preceded by at least 14 hours without exposure to workplace noise.”

> §1910.95(g)(7)(ii): “If the annual audiogram shows that an employee has suffered a standard threshold shift, the employer may obtain a retest within 30 days and consider the results of the retest as the annual audiogram.”

Paraphrased (not verbatim) supporting provisions:

- §1910.95(g)(5)(ii): the baseline may be established up to 12 months after first exposure where the employer uses a mobile test van for audiometric testing and the employee is provided with and uses hearing protectors between first exposure and the baseline test. **Excluded by the question, so the 6-month limit in (g)(5)(i) controls and the 12-month route is not available as a fallback.**
- §1910.95(g)(5)(iii), second sentence: the 14-hour requirement may be met by wearing hearing protectors that reduce the sound level below 85 dBA. **Excluded by the question, so actual absence of workplace noise exposure is required.**
- §1910.95(g)(10)(i): an STS is a change in hearing threshold relative to the baseline audiogram averaging 10 dB or more at 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz in either ear; (g)(10)(ii) allows an age correction.
- §1910.95(c): the action level is an 8-hour time-weighted average of 85 dBA.
- §1910.95(g)(6): annual audiograms for each employee exposed at or above the action level.
- §1910.95(g)(8)(i): written notice to the employee within 21 days of the determination of an STS (adjacent requirement, not one of the three answers).

**Paragraph-numbering correction.** The retest option is §1910.95(g)(7)(ii). §1910.95(g)(10) is the definition of the STS, not the retest rule. Any procedure, form or training slide that cites (g)(10) for the 30-day retest should be corrected.

## 3. Derivation and scope of each answer

### Ask 1 — 6 months

- Clock start: the date the employee’s exposure first reaches or exceeds the action level. Not the hire date (unless exposure begins at hire), not the date the monitoring report is signed, not the date the audiogram is scheduled.
- Because the mobile-van exception is excluded, the deadline is a hard 6 calendar months. Do not plan to 12 months.
- The baseline must be **valid**, not merely timely. An audiogram taken inside 6 months but without the (g)(5)(iii) quiet period, or with an uncalibrated or otherwise deficient test, does not discharge (g)(5)(i) and must be repeated.
- If the 6-month point has already passed when exposure is recognized: the obligation is already due. Establish the baseline immediately, document the cause of the delay, and in the interim enroll the employee in the hearing conservation program (protectors, training, annual audiometry). The 12-month van period cannot be applied retroactively.
- Annual audiograms follow the baseline (§1910.95(g)(6)); the 6-month baseline deadline and the annual cycle are separate obligations.

### Ask 2 — 14 hours

- The requirement is at least 14 hours without exposure to workplace noise immediately before the test that establishes the baseline.
- Because hearing protectors are not being used as the substitute permitted by the second sentence of (g)(5)(iii), the 14 hours must be actual absence of workplace noise exposure, not attenuated exposure.
- Implementation: schedule the baseline at the start of a shift following a full off-duty interval, and count back 14 hours from the appointment time. Example: test at 07:00 Tuesday means last workplace noise exposure no later than 17:00 Monday.
- Document the window with an employee attestation (no workplace noise; also no firearms, loud music, power tools or other high-level non-occupational noise, which is not regulated but degrades test validity). If the window is missed or doubtful, re-test; a non-compliant quiet period invalidates the baseline.
- If the program ever wants to count quiet on-site time (e.g., office duty) toward the 14 hours, obtain written confirmation from the enforcing authority before relying on it. This answer does not assume that.

### Ask 3 — 30 days

- Trigger: an **annual** audiogram shows an STS as defined in (g)(10). If there is no STS, (g)(7)(ii) does not apply and no retest window exists.
- The provision is permissive: the employer may obtain the retest and, if it does, the retest result is treated as the annual audiogram. If no retest is obtained, or it is obtained late, the original annual audiogram stands as the annual audiogram of record.
- Clock: 30 days from the date of the annual audiogram. It is not measured from the date the reviewer or professional supervisor determines that the shift is an STS; that review can lag, so the practical control is to compute the retest deadline on the day the audiogram is received.
- Consequential obligations if an STS stands: written notification to the employee within 21 days of the determination (§1910.95(g)(8)(i)); fit or refit and retrain on hearing protectors and, where applicable, further evaluation (§1910.95(g)(8)(ii)); recordkeeping (§1910.95(m)).

## 4. Implementation worksheet

Definitions:

- **D_base** = date of first exposure at or above the action level + 6 calendar months (same day-of-month; if that day does not exist in the target month, use the last day of the target month).
- **D_target** = D_base − 21 days (scheduling buffer so a failed quiet period or a no-show can still be re-tested before D_base).
- **D_retest** = date printed on the annual audiogram + 30 calendar days.

Worked examples:

| Event | Date | Computed deadline |
|---|---|---|
| First exposure at or above action level | 2024-03-01 | Baseline deadline 2024-09-01; target test date 2024-08-11 or earlier (e.g. week of 2024-08-05) |
| Same employee, hypothetical mobile-van route | — | 2025-03-01 — **not available in this program**, because the exception is not used |
| Baseline appointment | 2024-08-06, 07:00 | No workplace noise exposure after 2024-08-05, 17:00 |
| Annual audiogram shows STS | 2025-04-10 | Retest no later than 2025-05-10; if retest is done 2025-05-06, that result is the annual audiogram |
| STS determination made | 2025-04-15 | Written notice to employee no later than 2025-05-06 |

Procedure:

1. On or before the employee’s first exposure at or above the action level, record the exposure start date in the hearing conservation file.
2. Compute D_base and D_target; schedule the audiogram with the audiologist, otolaryngologist or physician (or certified technician) who performs the testing.
3. Issue the quiet-period instruction with the appointment, and obtain the attestation at the test.
4. On receipt of each annual audiogram, compare it to the baseline and apply (g)(10) the same day; if an STS is present, book the retest within 30 days and, if the retest is used, file it as the annual audiogram.
5. Retain the audiogram, the quiet-period attestation, the STS determination, the notification and the retest booking evidence for the duration of employment (§1910.95(m)).

## 5. Assumptions and limits

- Federal standard as of the July 1, 2014 edition; the three provisions quoted read the same in the current eCFR text retrieved for this analysis.
- No OSHA-approved State Plan variation is applied. State Plans may be identical to or more stringent than the federal rule; if the workplace is in a State Plan jurisdiction, verify the state text before relying on these numbers.
- The question’s exclusions are taken at face value: no mobile test van, and no hearing-protector substitution for the quiet period.
- The answers are the regulatory timeframes, not recommendations for a particular workplace; a program may adopt shorter internal targets (as in Section 4).
- This is a compliance analysis of the cited text, not legal advice.

verdict.summary:
## Answer

29 CFR § 1910.95, Table G-16 (Permissible Noise Exposures), July 1, 2014 edition, for constant levels measured on the A scale of a standard sound level meter at slow response:

| Sound level (dBA, slow response) | Permissible daily exposure duration |
|---|---|
| **90 dBA** | **8 hours** |
| **95 dBA** | **4 hours** |
| **100 dBA** | **2 hours** |

These are durations per 8-hour workday; they are the maximum time permitted at that steady level, not a target.

## Regulatory basis

§ 1910.95(c)(1) states the table's trigger and its measurement basis verbatim:

> "Protection against the effects of noise exposure shall be provided when the sound levels exceed those shown in Table G-16 when measured on the A scale of a standard sound level meter at slow response."

(Confirmed against the eCFR text of § 1910.95; the same sentence appears unchanged in the 2014 volume. "Slow response" and "A scale" are therefore conditions of the table's applicability, exactly as posed in the question.)

## Full Table G-16, with a consistency check

The three requested rows are part of a single monotonic table. Reproducing it in full, with the 5-dB exchange-rate computation that § 1910.95 Appendix A uses, confirms the table is internally consistent and that the requested rows are not special cases:

| Duration (hours) | Sound level (dBA, slow response) | T = 8 / 2^((L-90)/5) |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | 90 | 8.00 |
| 6 | 92 | 6.06 |
| 4 | 95 | 4.00 |
| 3 | 97 | 3.03 |
| 2 | 100 | 2.00 |
| 1.5 | 102 | 1.52 |
| 1 | 105 | 1.00 |
| 0.5 | 110 | 0.50 |
| 0.25 | 115 | 0.25 |

Every row agrees with the 5-dB exchange rate to the table's rounding, so 90→8, 95→4, 100→2 is the same rule the rest of the table follows. (This check is a verification aid; the durations quoted are the table entries, not values I computed.)

## Edition check (July 1, 2014)

Table G-16 has been unchanged since the 1983 hearing-conservation revision of § 1910.95; the July 1, 2014 print and the current eCFR carry identical rows. To confirm against the specific edition named in the request, open the GovInfo annual CFR volume for that year — `CFR-2014-title29-vol5`, § 1910.95 — and read Table G-16 at the end of the section. The values will be the three above.

## Application notes (where a reader could go wrong)

1. **Constant level only.** The 8/4/2 figures apply to a steady level held for the whole exposure period. If the day is made up of periods at different levels, do **not** pick the loudest row; use the fraction rule in the footnote to the 90 dBA row: sum C1/T1 + C2/T2 + ... over each period (C = actual time at that level, T = the table duration for that level), and the exposure is compliant only if the sum is ≤ 1.
2. **Exchange rate.** This standard uses a **5-dB** exchange rate (a 5 dBA increase halves the permitted time). Do not substitute the 3-dB rate used by some other standards and consensus criteria — that would give 4 hours at 93 dBA and other values that do not exist in Table G-16.
3. **Table vs. computation.** Table G-16 is discrete; § 1910.95 Appendix A gives the continuous dose/D = 100 × (C1/T1 + ...) computation and the TLV-style formula for levels between rows. Use Appendix A for a level not printed in the table; use Table G-16 for the printed rows.
4. **Impulse/noise peaks.** Table G-16's duration column does not cover impact or impulse noise; § 1910.95(b)(1) separately caps impulsive noise at 140 dB peak sound pressure level.
5. **Protection is not a substitute in the table.** These durations are the exposure limit; hearing protectors, if required when the limit is exceeded, are addressed by the hearing-conservation and attenuation provisions (§ 1910.95(b), (i), (j)) and do not change the table entries.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER (headline)

- Ask 1 — Minimum unlocking strength for tagout-device attachment means: 50 pounds (a floor: 'no less than 50 pounds').
- Ask 2 — Frequency of employer inspection of the energy-control procedure: at least annually, i.e. a maximum interval of 1 year (12 months).
- Ask 3 (format) — Both are given above in the regulation's own terms: the strength in pounds, and the inspection interval in years/months.

Standard: 29 CFR § 1910.147, The control of hazardous energy (lockout/tagout), Subpart J.


1. TAGOUT-DEVICE ATTACHMENT MEANS — 50 POUNDS

Controlling text (quoted verbatim):

  "Tagout device attachment means shall be of a non-reusable type, attachable by hand, self-locking, and non-releasable with a minimum unlocking strength of no less than 50 pounds and having the general design and basic characteristics of being at least equivalent to a one-piece, all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie."

Citation: § 1910.147(c)(5) — Lockout devices and tagout devices — specifically the "Substantial" requirement of (c)(5)(i). The sentence is most commonly reproduced as § 1910.147(c)(5)(i)(C)(2); some compilations render it (c)(5)(ii)(C). Locate it by the quoted sentence text; the text, not the letter, is what governs, and the designator should be confirmed against the print volume as described in § 5 below.

What the requirement means in practice:

- The 50 pounds is a MINIMUM UNLOCKING STRENGTH — the force needed to release or defeat the attachment means. It is a floor, not a target and not a ceiling. A device that releases at, say, 30 pounds does not comply; a device that releases at 60 pounds complies on this element.
- It applies to the ATTACHMENT MEANS (the tie, strap, wire, etc. by which the tag is fixed to the energy-isolating device), not to the tag itself and not to lockout devices. There is no numeric pound rating anywhere in § 1910.147 for lockout hardware; lockout devices are governed by the qualitative "substantial … prevent removal without the use of excessive force or unusual techniques" test. Do not carry the 50-pound number over to lockout devices, and do not accept a lockout device as a substitute for evaluating tagout attachment means.
- The same sentence imposes four concurrent design characteristics, all of which must be met in addition to the 50-pound floor: non-reusable; attachable by hand (no tools required to apply); self-locking; non-releasable. "Attachable by hand" and "non-releasable with a minimum unlocking strength of no less than 50 pounds" are deliberately paired: the means must go on easily by hand but must not come off by hand at low force.
- The performance benchmark is a one-piece, all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie — general design and basic characteristics at least equivalent to that.
- Purchasing/specification consequence: tag attachment hardware should be procured against a stated minimum unlocking strength of 50 lb (or greater) with the non-reusable, hand-attachable, self-locking, non-releasable characteristics; a generic "cable tie" or reusable hook-and-loop strap does not establish compliance on its face.
- Supplementary (NOT part of the regulation): 50 lbf is approximately 222.4 N (50 x 4.44822). The regulatory unit is pounds; use pounds in procedures, specifications and audits.


2. PERIODIC INSPECTION OF THE ENERGY-CONTROL PROCEDURE — AT LEAST ANNUALLY (MAX 12 MONTHS)

Controlling text (quoted verbatim):

  "The employer shall conduct a periodic inspection of the energy control procedure at least annually to ensure that the procedure and the requirements of this standard are being followed."

Citation: § 1910.147(c)(6)(i) — Periodic inspection.

What the requirement means in practice:

- "At least annually" sets a MAXIMUM interval of 12 months. It is a ceiling on the interval, not a minimum, and § 1910.147 contains no provision allowing the interval to be extended beyond 12 months (no conditional or risk-based extension exists in this standard). A calendar-based schedule that never lets any procedure go more than 12 months between inspections satisfies the text; a schedule with any gap exceeding 12 months does not.
- Scope is the energy-control PROCEDURE(S), i.e. the written procedure for the machine/equipment/process — this is a procedure-and-practice audit, not a hardware inventory or a device condition check. It must verify both the procedure and adherence to the standard.
- Independence: the inspection must be performed by an authorized employee other than the one(s) using the procedure being inspected.
- Required content (same paragraph): correct any deviations or inadequacies identified; where lockout is used, a review between the inspector and each authorized employee of that employee's responsibilities under the procedure; where tagout is used, a review between the inspector and each affected AND authorized employee of that employee's responsibilities under the procedure and the limitations imposed by the tagout program.
- Certification: the employer must certify that the periodic inspections were performed, identifying the machine or equipment on which the procedure was being utilized, the date of the inspection, the employees included, and the person performing the inspection. The certification is the record that makes the annual interval auditable; without it the interval cannot be evidenced to an inspector.
- Interaction with training: findings from this inspection trigger additional retraining under (c)(7)(iv) where deviations or inadequacies in employees' knowledge or use of the procedure are revealed. The annual obligation is the inspection; retraining is event-driven, not annual.
- Programme consequence: the annual inspection interval is per energy-control procedure and must be tracked as such (a procedure register with last-inspection date, next-due date at +12 months, inspector, and affected/authorized employees reviewed).


3. FORMAT COMPLIANCE (Ask 3)

Strength stated in the regulation's pounds unit: 50 pounds (no less than).
Inspection interval stated: at least annually — maximum interval of 1 year (12 months).


4. WHAT THIS DELIVERABLE DOES NOT SAY (guard against over-reading)

- It does not state or imply any numeric unlocking-strength requirement for lockout devices.
- It does not state that inspections may be spaced beyond 12 months, and no such extension should be written into a procedure on the authority of this standard.
- It does not treat 50 pounds as a target design value or a maximum; it is the floor.


5. GROUNDING AND VERIFICATION NOTE (disclosed, not a blocker)

- The verbatim sentence for the 50-pound requirement and the verbatim sentence for the annual inspection were verified against the currently published text of § 1910.147 (eCFR, https://ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1910/subpart-J/section-1910.147, fetched 2026-11-15, sha256 fc27bc35e0ff; consistent with OSHA's published standard page and OSHA Publication 3120).
- I did not open a page image of the July 1, 2014 GPO print volume in this pass. Both provisions are long-standing (final rule, 54 FR 36644, Sept. 1, 1989, effective 1990) and neither has been amended in substance; the current text still carries both sentences exactly as quoted. The values therefore answer the question for the July 1, 2014 edition as well as for the current text.
- If edition-exact provenance is required for a compliance file, confirm in one step: govinfo.gov, Code of Federal Regulations, 2014 edition, Title 29 (Labor), Part 1910, § 1910.147, and compare the two quoted sentences and the paragraph designators (the 50-pound sentence sits in the "Substantial" requirement of (c)(5)(i); the inspection sentence is (c)(6)(i)). If the 2014 print text differs in any respect, the 2014 text controls for an edition-specific answer; on the record available, it does not differ.


6. SAFETY-ENGINEER APPLICATION CHECKLIST

1) Procedure register: every energy-control procedure listed with last inspection date and a next-due date hard-capped at +12 months; no procedure permitted to exceed 12 months.
2) Inspector assignment control: inspector must be an authorized employee who does not use the procedure being inspected; record the assignment.
3) Inspection content template: procedure accuracy + field adherence; lockout — responsibilities review with each authorized employee; tagout — responsibilities AND tagout-program limitations review with each affected and authorized employee; deviations logged and corrected.
4) Certification record per inspection: machine/equipment, date, employees included, person performing. Retain so the annual interval is demonstrable.
5) Tagout hardware specification: attachment means specified as non-reusable, hand-attachable, self-locking, non-releasable, minimum unlocking strength no less than 50 lb, at least equivalent in design to a one-piece all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie; verify at receipt and during the annual inspection.
6) Do not extend intervals or substitute lockout-hardware language for the tagout attachment-means requirement.
